newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Post-holiday doldrums seen.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Post-holiday doldrums seen.

text.p: Post-holiday trading of U.S. government securities was expected to remain in the doldrums Thursday amid a dearth of economic data and active players.
Analysts expected Treasury prices to stay in the same narrow bands they have traded in all week and no pickup in activity was seen until next week.
Weekly initial jobless claims were slated for release Thursday, and Friday will see the monthly release of durable goods data, neither of which were viewed as market-moving numbers.

"It's dead as a doornail with a lot of people out on vacation. Durable goods will come out on Friday, but that won't attract too much attention," said Suzanne Rizzo, domestic economist at Maria Fiorini Ramirez Inc.
"I doubt too many people will come into the office just for that number. This is a good time to take some time off and relax," she added.
Economists generally foresaw a slight gain in November durable goods orders above the October rise of 0.3 percent.
"The market's still in a holiday mood and there won't be too many people around. Staffing will remain skeletal," said Don Fine, chief market analyst with Chase Asset Management.
Fine noted that London markets will be closed in observance of Boxing Day in the United Kingdom, putting a further damper on trading activity.
"Even with an unexpectedly higher or lower initial claims report on Thursday, there won't be too many people here to react," Fine said.
"The only risk is that in a very, very thin market a big buy or sell order can move things around," he added.

"It's a tough call right now. The market's really trading in very tight ranges," said Victor Zoppa, senior vice president and director of fixed-income research at Gruntal & Co. "We may be seeing an uptrend in the short term, but a slightly lower long-term trend," he added.
However, Zoppa acknowledged that the market continues to trade in very tight ranges and probably would do so for the remainder of the week.
"No one wants to make a commitment at the end of the year and get caught one way or the other," Zoppa said.

In late action on Tuesday, the two-year note was at 99-27/32, up 1/32 to yield 5.83 percent. The 10-year note was at 101-05/32, up 1/32 to yield 6.33 percent. The 30-year bond was unchanged at 98-28/32 to yield 6.58 percent.
The overnight bank lending or federal funds rate was expected to open between 5-1/4 percent and 5-3/8 percent on Thursday.
U.S. credit markets closed Wednesday for the Christmas holiday.
